explanation: Double-quoted strings process escape sequences and interpolate variables, while single-quoted strings do not (except \').
The ?? (null coalescing) operator uses isset()-like semantics, so it returns null for undefined variables without emitting any notice or warning.
echo accepts multiple comma-separated arguments and outputs them in order, so 'a' followed by 'b' prints ab.
In PHP, print always returns 1, so it can be used within expressions, unlike echo.
The Elvis operator returns the left operand when it is truthy, and the right operand only when the left is falsy.
PHP 8 lowered the '.' operator's precedence so it now binds weaker than '+' and '-', e.g. "a" . 1 + 2 is evaluated as "a" . (1 + 2).
The ** operator in PHP is right-associative, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 equals 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 512, not 64.
In PHP 8 the '.' operator has lower precedence than '+', so it evaluates as 'sum: ' . (2 + 3).
With ===, arrays must have the same key/value pairs in the same order with identical types, so element order matters.
The == operator is a loose comparison, and 0 == false evaluates to true because PHP converts false to 0.
Since PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string to a number converts the number to a string instead, so "abc" == 0 is false.
In PHP, null == 0, null == "", and null == false all evaluate to true under loose comparison.
Casting a string to int parses the leading numeric portion, so '42abc' becomes 42.
PHP converts the numeric string '5' to the integer 5 during arithmetic, so 5 + 5 equals 10.
In PHP, false casts to an empty string "", while true casts to "1".
Due to IEEE 754 floating-point precision, 0.1 + 0.2 yields 0.30000000000000004441..., which is not strictly equal to the literal 0.3.
strrev() reverses the string byte-by-byte, so multi-byte UTF-8 characters get corrupted instead of properly reversed.
str_contains() returns true because 'world' is found within 'Hello world'.
str_pad() accepts STR_PAD_RIGHT (default), STR_PAD_LEFT, or STR_PAD_BOTH, so padding is not limited to the right side.
By default trim() strips whitespace characters including spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, NUL bytes, and vertical tabs.
strlen counts bytes, and 'é' is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 1+2+1+1+1 = 6.
A negative start of -3 counts from the end of the string, returning the last three characters 'def'.
ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character uppercased; PHP strings are immutable and are not modified in place.
Heredoc (<<<EOT) parses variables like a double-quoted string, while nowdoc (<<<'EOT') treats the text literally with no interpolation.
sort() reindexes the array with new numeric keys, discarding original key associations (use asort() to preserve them).
PHP automatically casts numeric string array keys containing valid integers (like '5') to the integer type.
in_array() uses loose (==) comparison by default; strict === comparison requires setting the third $strict parameter to true.
When called without a callback, array_filter() removes all entries that evaluate to false (e.g., 0, "0", "", null, false, and empty arrays).
array_slice() reindexes numeric keys by default; keys are only preserved when the fourth parameter $preserve_keys is set to true (string keys are always kept).
array_slice takes 2 elements starting at index 1, returning [20, 30].
The + union operator keeps the left array's 'a' key and adds the missing 'b' key, resulting in ['a' => 1, 'b' => 2] with 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 added support for unpacking arrays with string keys using the spread operator, whereas before only integer-keyed arrays were allowed.
Since PHP 8, named arguments can be freely mixed with argument unpacking, e.g. foo(...$args, c: 3), where string keys in $args become named arguments.
PHP anonymous functions do not automatically inherit outer scope variables; they must be explicitly imported via the `use` keyword.
func_num_args() returns the actual number of arguments passed to the function (3), not the number of declared parameters.
PHP arrow functions (fn) only allow a single expression that is implicitly returned; unlike regular functions or JS arrow functions, they cannot contain multiple statements in curly braces.
PHP arrow functions automatically capture outer variables by value, and the capture happens at creation time, not lazily at use time.
Static closures cannot automatically bind $this from the enclosing scope, and attempting to use $this inside them causes an error.
The closure captures $x by value at creation time, so changing $x afterward doesn't affect it.
In coercive typing mode PHP automatically converts numeric strings like "5" to int when passed to an int parameter.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing visibility modifiers in constructor parameters to automatically declare and assign properties.
In PHP, declaring a method with the final keyword forbids subclasses from overriding it.
In PHP, declaring a method final prevents subclasses from overriding it.
Private members of a parent class are only accessible within that class itself; subclasses must use protected or public visibility to inherit access.
Anonymous classes are named 'class@anonymous', followed by a NUL byte, the file path, line number, and a counter.
Private methods are not inherited or visible to child classes, so a child can freely declare a same-named method with any visibility without a visibility-conflict error.
__get() is called for inaccessible (private or protected) properties as well as non-existent ones, not only for non-existent properties.
Modifying a readonly property after initialization throws an Error (e.g., 'Cannot modify readonly property'), not an Exception.
PHP interfaces may declare constants, which work like class constants (and can be overridden by implementing classes since PHP 8.1).
The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a given class, interface, or one of its parent classes.
PHP interfaces may declare static methods, which implementing classes must define as static.
instanceof also returns true when the object's class implements the given interface (directly or via inheritance).
In PHP, interface methods can only declare signatures (no body); default implementations are only possible with traits or abstract classes.
Abstract methods may be declared public or protected, but not private, since they must be visible to overriding child classes.
Foo::cases() returns an array containing all cases defined in the enum, which are A, B, and C.
Since PHP 8.2, traits can declare constants, which become available to classes that use the trait.
In PHP 7+, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, allowing them to be caught with catch (Throwable $e).
TypeError extends Error, and Error and Exception are separate branches that both implement Throwable, so a catch (Exception) block does not catch TypeError.
The @ operator only suppresses errors and warnings, not exceptions, which must be caught with try/catch.
Since PHP 7, intdiv() throwing on division by zero raises a DivisionByZeroError (an ArithmeticError subclass), not a warning or exception.
The finally block always executes, regardless of whether an exception was thrown, caught, or left uncaught.
An exception thrown in a finally block overrides any return value or pending exception from the try/catch and propagates instead.
In PHP, all objects are always truthy, so casting any object to bool yields true.
Shutdown functions registered with register_shutdown_function() execute when the script terminates, including termination via exit().
The use statement only creates an alias for the class name; the file is loaded later when the class is actually used (typically via autoloading).
In PHP namespaces, `use function` imports functions while `use const` imports constants.
PSR-4 strips the 'App\' prefix and maps the remaining namespace path 'Controller\Api\UserController' to src/Controller/Api/UserController.php.
Composer's vendor/autoload.php ultimately calls spl_autoload_register() to register its autoloader function/class loader.
__NAMESPACE__ is a magic constant that holds the name of the current namespace (e.g., 'App\Controllers'), and an empty string in the global namespace.
An unqualified class name in new is resolved relative to the current namespace (after applying imports/aliases), not from the global root.
PSR-4 replaces the namespace prefix App\ with the base directory src/, so App\Model\User maps to src/Model/User.php.
Namespace import `use` statements may only appear at the top level of a file or namespace block, not inside a function body (the closure `use ($var)` clause is a different feature).
In PHP, assigning an array to another variable copies its values (objects are the ones handled by reference).
PHP arrays are assigned by value, so appending to $b doesn't affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
PHP functions have local scope, so user-defined globals are only visible inside via the global keyword, $GLOBALS, or parameters.
unset($GLOBALS['x']) removes the variable from the global symbol table entirely, affecting all scopes, unlike unset($x) which only unsets the local copy.
$x is passed by reference, so incrementing it directly modifies $n from 5 to 6.
A by-value foreach iterates over a copy (snapshot) of the array, so modifications to the original array inside the loop do not affect the iteration.
Static properties belong to the class itself and are shared by all instances, so a change via one object is visible to all others.
PHP casts boolean array keys to integers, so true becomes key 1 (and false becomes 0), never stored as bool.
Since PHP 7, a generator may return a final value with `return`, retrievable via `$gen->getReturn()` once the generator has finished.
Once a generator has begun executing (even if fully consumed), calling rewind() throws an Exception; it only works before iteration starts.
In PHP, yield from delegates iteration to another generator, Traversable object, or array, forwarding values and return values.
Calling a function containing yield returns a Generator object, whose class name is Generator.
The generator yields all three values from the array via yield from, so iterator_to_array produces a 3-element array.
SplStack implements a LIFO stack, not a FIFO queue; SplQueue is the FIFO class.
ArrayIterator wraps an array (or object) and implements the Iterator interface, allowing traversal with foreach or iterator methods like next() and current().
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so foreach can iterate over it.
password_hash() generates a cryptographically secure salt itself and embeds it in the returned hash, so manually passing a salt is unnecessary (and the salt option was removed in PHP 7).
In PHP 8, PASSWORD_DEFAULT currently uses bcrypt (not md5) with an automatically generated salt.
password_verify() checks the plaintext password against the hash and returns true (boolean), since 'secret' matches the generated hash.
strip_tags() only removes HTML/PHP tags from a string; preventing SQL injection requires escaping or prepared statements, e.g. with PDO or mysqli_real_escape_string().
Calling session_regenerate_id() after login replaces the session ID, preventing attackers from using a pre-set (fixed) session identifier.
php_sapi_name() returns a lowercase string describing the Server API, such as 'cli' or 'fpm-fcgi'.
session_destroy() removes the session data from server storage but leaves the session cookie in the browser, which must be cleared separately (e.g., with setcookie() expired).
The $_SESSION array is only populated after session_start() is called (or session.auto_start is enabled); otherwise it remains empty.
The array_find() function returns the first element of an array that matches a given callback and was added in PHP 8.4.
Property hooks (get/set declared directly on a property) were introduced by the Property Hooks RFC in PHP 8.4.
PHP 8.4 introduced asymmetric visibility, allowing separate read/write scopes like public private(set).
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute, which marks function return values as intended to be consumed, was introduced in PHP 8.5.
The pipe operator |> was introduced in PHP 8.5 via the pipe operator RFC, allowing function chaining like $x |> fn($y).
The clone-with syntax, e.g. clone($obj, ['x' => 1]), was introduced in PHP 8.4 via the 'Clone with' RFC.
The array_first() and array_last() functions were accepted via RFC and introduced in PHP 8.5.
The Partial Function Application v2 RFC was voted in and adopted for PHP 8.5 in 2025.
The clamp_v2 RFC adding the clamp() function was accepted and implemented in PHP 8.5.
The Context Managers v2 RFC has not been adopted into PHP, so no such feature exists in the language as of that date.
The Bound-Erased Generic Types RFC, which proposed generics via type erasure, failed to reach acceptance when voted on in 2026.
PHP remains single-threaded per request; ZTS/multithreading is still an optional build mode and no accepted RFC has made it the default.
PHP 8.5 does not include generics; parameterized types remain unimplemented despite long-running RFC discussions.
As of 2026-11-07, PHP 8.5 is the latest stable release and PHP 8.6's GA (2026-11-19) hasn't occurred yet.
The PHP 6 branch (an aborted Unicode rewrite) never produced a stable release, and PHP 5.6 was followed directly by PHP 7.0 in 2015.
The RFC to add the #[\Deprecated] attribute for marking deprecated functions, methods, and class constants was approved and implemented in PHP 8.4.
Both clean and onion architectures enforce that dependencies point inward, so inner layers (domain/core) have no knowledge of outer layers.

Domain entities should be framework-agnostic plain PHP objects, depending only on the language and its standard library so the domain layer stays decoupled from infrastructure like Doctrine or Symfony.
Controllers and Twig templates are part of the delivery/presentation layer; merely invoking use cases does not make them business logic.

The onion architecture places the domain model (entities and business rules) at the very center, with outer layers like domain services, application services, and infrastructure/UI wrapping around it.
Tools like deptrac analyze class dependencies against defined layer rules and exit with an error when a forbidden cross-layer call is detected.
A use case should receive plain data (e.g., DTOs/primitive values), not framework or infrastructure objects like HTTP requests or EntityManager, so it stays decoupled and testable.
A repository provides a collection-like interface for accessing aggregates/entities while hiding the underlying storage mechanism.
Clean architecture's dependency rule makes the database an infrastructure detail hidden behind interfaces, so only the outer layer's adapter implementations change.

An aggregate in DDD is a cluster of domain objects (entities and value objects) treated as a single consistency unit with an aggregate root, which is a domain modeling concept rather than a database table.
A Value Object is defined by being immutable and by equality based on its field values rather than object identity.
In Domain-Driven Design, the aggregate root is the single external entry point of an aggregate through which all modifications must pass.
In DDD, only aggregate roots get repositories, since the aggregate is the unit of persistence and internal entities are only reachable through the root.
In Domain-Driven Design, the ubiquitous language is the shared vocabulary of the model used consistently by both developers and domain experts.
It's a paradigm (in Kuhn's sense): inside it, a model and its language are mutually consistent, while outside the same words refer to different models.
DDD recommends a rich domain model where entities contain behavior and business logic, making the anemic model (logic in services) an anti-pattern.

In DDD, a bounded context defines a boundary within which a model applies, so a concept like Customer is modeled as separate classes in different contexts, each with only the attributes relevant there.
The Symfony service container instantiates a service only when it is actually requested or injected, so services are lazy by default.
The Symfony console command `php bin/console debug:router` lists all registered routes.
Symfony automatically registers and autowires services (e.g., everything in src/) by default, so manual declarations are rarely needed.
Twig compiles each template into an optimized PHP class and stores it in a cache directory, so compilation only happens once rather than on every request.
In dev, Symfony checks timestamps of tracked resources and reuses the cached container unless one of them changed.
Symfony reads the APP_ENV environment variable (defined in .env) to determine whether it runs in the dev or prod environment.
Symfony can only route to public methods; private (or protected) methods are not accessible as controller actions.
Subscribers are just a convenient way to register listeners; they have no built-in priority and can even be ordered after listeners or per-event priority settings.
Symfony 6.0 removed the legacy Guard authenticator system, so authentication is now handled solely by classes implementing AuthenticatorInterface.
Symfony's #[IsGranted] attribute on a controller method checks roles/permissions via the security voter system and throws an AccessDeniedException (HTTP 403) when the requirement fails.
Symfony security voters implement VoterInterface to decide if a user is granted an attribute (e.g. 'EDIT') on a specific object (e.g. $post), checked via isGranted() or security attributes.
Symfony 7 requires PHP 8.2+, where native attributes replace the deprecated doctrine/annotations library, which is no longer supported.
Symfony's Form component enables CSRF protection by default, automatically adding a _token field and validating it when the form is submitted.
Symfony constraints always trigger server-side validation on submission; HTML5 attributes are merely a client-side convenience and can be bypassed.
The MakerBundle's `make:form` command generates a new form class (FormType).
Symfony only stores encoded/hashed credentials (and modern versions store none at all), never the password in plain text.
Symfony stores each bundle's configuration in its own YAML/PHP/XML file under config/packages, such as framework.yaml, twig.yaml, or doctrine.yaml.
By convention (e.g., Symfony), .env holds safe default values and is committed, while .env.local with real secrets is gitignored.
The `debug:container` console command displays all services registered in the dependency injection container along with their aliases.
The compiled container is frozen at build time, so calling setParameter() at runtime throws a LogicException.
Since Symfony 3.4, services are private by default (public: false) and can only be used via injection, not fetched directly from the container.
Bundles work without configuration because they provide default settings via their Extension/Configuration classes; config in config/packages only overrides those defaults.
In Symfony, environment variables are referenced in services.yaml using the %env(VAR)% syntax, which resolves the value at runtime.
Symfony uses the APP_DEBUG environment variable (typically set to 1 in .env) to toggle debug mode, which controls the profiler, error pages, and Twig debugging.
Symfony Messenger allows a message to be handled by multiple handlers, and all of them are executed when the message is dispatched on the bus.
The sync transport executes the message handler immediately in the same process/request, unlike async transports which queue messages for a worker.
Symfony Messenger provides the `php bin/console messenger:consume` command to start the worker that consumes and processes queued messages.
In Symfony Messenger, retry_strategy (max_retries, delay, multiplier, etc.) is configured individually under each transport in framework.messenger.transports.

Symfony Messenger's default serializer uses PHP's native serialize()/unserialize() (PhpSerializer), not JSON; JSON serialization requires configuring a custom serializer such as the Symfony serializer with JSON format.
The Symfony Scheduler component generates scheduled messages (e.g., tick messages) and relies on Messenger transports/buses to dispatch and handle them.
The Messenger 'doctrine' transport stores queued messages in database tables managed through Doctrine ORM/DBAL.
Symfony Messenger allows custom middleware to be configured in the buses' middleware list, either before or after the built-in middleware such as handle_message.
Symfony follows a fixed release schedule where major versions (x.0) are released every two years in November, and minor versions (x.y) every six months, in May and November.
Symfony 8.0 (released November 2025) requires PHP 8.4 or higher.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for docblock annotations entirely; developers must use PHP 8 native attributes for routes, validation, etc.
Symfony's AssetMapper component serves and versions CSS/JS directly using an importmap.php file, eliminating the need for Node.js or webpack.
Symfony 6.4 is an LTS (Long-Term Support) release, with security fixes until November 2028.
Symfony removes deprecated features in the next major release, so when you upgrade to a new major version the previous branch's deprecated code is gone and you must have fixed all deprecations first.
Symfony ships an UPGRADE file (e.g., UPGRADING-x.0.md) with each major release documenting breaking changes and how to migrate.
The Symfony AssetMapper component serves and version-manages JavaScript/CSS assets and handles JavaScript importmaps natively, eliminating the need for Node.js or Webpack (Webpack Encore).
Symfony 8.2 follows the November release cycle and is scheduled for late November 2026, after November 7.
Symfony follows a six-month release cycle, with 8.0 in November 2025, 8.1 in May 2026, and 8.2 scheduled for November 2026.
Following Symfony's release schedule, 8.1 (May 2026) is followed by 8.2, released in November 2026.

Symfony follows semantic versioning and backward compatibility promises: minor releases like 8.2 never break compatibility, and even major upgrades are gradual, never requiring full application rewrites.
Minor releases within a major version (like 8.1 → 8.2) are designed to be backward compatible, introducing only new features and deprecations rather than requiring code changes.
Following Symfony's release cycle (like 6.4 before 7.0), the last minor release of the 8.x branch is 8.4, an LTS version released just before Symfony 9.0.
Symfony 8.x requires PHP 8.4 or later, so PHP 8.5 is not a requirement.
Symfony's policy guarantees that any feature deprecated in the 8.x branch remains in place throughout the entire 8.x series and is only removed in the next major version, Symfony 9.0.
Twig is sandboxed: {{ }} can only use registered functions, filters, and whitelisted methods, not arbitrary PHP code.
Twig's Environment enables autoescaping with the 'html' strategy by default, so printed variables are escaped unless escaped via |raw or the autoescape tag.
Twig's |e filter escapes a string using the 'html' strategy by default, making it safe to output in an HTML context.
The twig/intl-extra package provides the format_number filter, which formats numbers according to a given locale using ICU/intl.
The raw filter marks a value as safe, so Twig's auto-escaping will not escape it.
{{ }} outputs the value of an expression, while {% %} delimits Twig logic tags such as if, for, and set.
Twig allows declaring variables inside a template using the {% set %} tag, e.g. {% set foo = 'bar' %}.
Twig's dump() function outputs the structure and values of a variable (like arrays or objects), typically used with the Twig debug extension enabled.
Bootstrap provides prebuilt CSS styles and JS components for styling pages, while SPA frameworks like Angular or React handle application structure and routing.
In Bootstrap, the .container class creates a responsive fixed-width container whose max-width changes at each breakpoint.
Bootstrap's grid splits each row into 12 columns, not 16, though it is indeed built on CSS floats.
Bootstrap 5 has six breakpoints, but xs requires no infix, so the class-name infixes are sm, md, lg, xl, xxl — five in total.
In Bootstrap, spacing utilities like .mt-3 or .px-2 derive their size from the $spacer variable, where the number is that multiple of $spacer.
In Bootstrap 5, interactive components are enabled via the data-bs-toggle attribute (e.g. data-bs-toggle="dropdown"), replacing Bootstrap 4's data-toggle.
Bootstrap 5 dropped jQuery as a dependency, so its components work with plain vanilla JavaScript.
Bootstrap 5.3 enables dark mode via the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on the root element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine requires you to create the schema explicitly (e.g., via migrations or the SchemaTool); it never creates tables automatically at runtime.
EntityManager::persist() tells Doctrine to manage a new entity, deferring any INSERT SQL until flush() is called.
EntityManager::merge() was removed in Doctrine ORM 3 (it was deprecated in 2.x), so this method no longer exists.
DQL (Doctrine Query Language) operates at the object model level, so it references entities, associations, and fields, which Doctrine then translates to SQL over tables and columns.
Doctrine's Repository::find() returns null when no entity matches the given id.
DoctrineBundle never flushes automatically; you must call flush() yourself or pending changes are discarded when the entity manager closes at the end of the request.
Doctrine's Unit of Work detects changes to managed entities, so flush() alone commits them; persist() is only needed for new entities.
In Doctrine ORM, remove() only schedules the entity for deletion; the DELETE SQL is executed when flush() is called.
MVCC in PostgreSQL is specifically designed so that readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers; they work on different versions of rows.
The EXPLAIN statement (e.g., EXPLAIN SELECT ...) shows the query execution plan without actually running the query.

SERIAL is a legacy, non-standard shorthand that just creates a sequence-backed DEFAULT, whereas GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY is the SQL-standard identity column with stricter semantics (e.g., GENERATED ALWAYS blocks explicit value inserts without OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE).
PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct from each other, so a UNIQUE constraint permits multiple rows with NULL in the column.
PostgreSQL's string_agg(value, separator) aggregate concatenates strings using the given delimiter.
Plain VACUUM only marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table files; only VACUUM FULL compacts the table and returns space to the operating system.
In a window function's OVER clause, PARTITION BY divides the rows into groups (partitions) over which the function is computed.
READ COMMITTED only prevents dirty reads; each new read in a transaction can still see committed changes from other transactions, so non-repeatable reads are still possible.
Without an explicit BEGIN, PostgreSQL executes each statement in its own implicit transaction that is committed immediately, which is autocommit behavior.
The COMMIT command ends a transaction and permanently saves all its changes to the database.
Indexes also help UPDATE and DELETE because their WHERE clause can locate the affected rows quickly via the index.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT to roll back part of a transaction without aborting the whole transaction.
Plain EXPLAIN shows the plan without running the query, while EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query to report real timings and row counts.
pgvector is the open-source PostgreSQL extension that provides a vector data type and indexes (IVFFlat, HNSW) for similarity search on embeddings.
A partial index indexes only the table rows that satisfy the WHERE predicate, making it smaller and faster for queries that match that condition.
PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE via Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which detects serialization anomalies rather than locking the rows a transaction reads.
HTTP 201 is the 'Created' status, indicating the request succeeded and a new resource was created.
HTTP 204 No Content indicates the request succeeded but there is no body to return, commonly used after DELETE.
RFC 9110 (and earlier RFC 7231) defines DELETE as an idempotent method, since repeating the request has the same intended effect as performing it once.
Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a response header sent by the server (the client sends the Origin header instead).
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests is specifically used to indicate the client has sent too many requests in a given time, i.e., exceeded a rate limit.
It's the reverse: 4xx codes indicate client errors, while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.
The Content-Type header specifies the MIME type of the request or response body.
RFC 5789 defines PATCH as not necessarily idempotent, whereas PUT is required to be idempotent.
Plain == should be avoided because password verification should use password_verify() (or hash_equals()) to prevent timing attacks and handle algorithm formats correctly.
A CSRF token is generated by the server, stored in the session, embedded in forms, and validated server-side on state-changing requests like POST to prevent cross-site request forgery.
The standard HTTP response header used to deliver a CSP policy is Content-Security-Policy.
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, not authentication; access tokens represent delegated permissions and don't reliably identify a user (that's OpenID Connect's role).
XSS is prevented by properly escaping/encoding output when displaying data (e.g., htmlspecialchars), not merely by validating input before storing it in the database.
The authorization server appends the authorization code as the 'code' parameter to the redirect_uri, and the client then exchanges it for an access token.
Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials issued alongside short-lived access tokens specifically so a client can request new access tokens without re-authenticating the user.
Salts are not secret; they are stored alongside the hash (e.g., in bcrypt output) and are needed to recompute and verify the password.
PHPUnit only recognizes and runs test methods in classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase, so extending it is required.
setUp() runs before each test method; the method that runs once before all tests is setUpBeforeClass().
A data provider supplies multiple sets of arguments, causing the test to run once per set.
In PHPUnit, $this->expectException(ClassName::class) declares that the tested code is expected to throw an exception of that class.
It's the reverse: a mock verifies which methods were called, while a stub only provides canned return values without verification.
PHPUnit 10 introduced metadata attributes, and #[DataProvider] is the recommended replacement for the deprecated @dataProvider annotation.
PHPUnit supports test dependencies via the depends attribute (e.g., #[Depends] or @depends), allowing one test to receive the return value of another.
PHPUnit orders tests randomly with the --order-by=random command-line option (seed can be fixed via --random-order-seed).
